summary: Libya's eVisa portal lists the tourist visa with an "Apply now" link and says the sponsor (the tourism company) must be registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority; for its other visa types it says online applications are not open yet. The portal's country list marks Algeria, Malaysia, Mauritania and Tunisia as fully exempt and Türkiye as partially exempt. The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Libya except the cities of Tripoli, Misrata, and Benghazi, Al-Bayda, Derna and the surrounding Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those cities.

currencyLimits.text: The UK Foreign Office says that if you enter or leave Libya with over USD 10,000-worth of cash, you must declare it to the customs authorities, or you risk having the money confiscated and even being detained, and that it is illegal to take dinar out of Libya.

notes: The Government of Canada says Libyan authorities strictly prohibit the import and/or export of certain goods, including alcohol, religious material and antiquities, weapons, illegal drugs, pork and pork products, and pornographic content. The UK Foreign Office says it is illegal in Libya to drink alcohol.

The UK Foreign Office says you must get permission before taking any photographs at or near military facilities; the Government of Canada says photography of military installations, personnel and government buildings is prohibited, and to seek permission before taking photos of official buildings or individuals.

postArrivalRegistration.penaltyText: The UK government says you could get a fine when you leave the country if you do not register.
postArrivalRegistration.text: The UK government says all short-stay visitors must register with the police within a week of arrival, and that not registering could bring a fine on departure. The Australian government says travellers must register their passport with a police station on arrival, at the station closest to where they stay if it is safe to do so, and that failing to do so may result in fines and problems during the stay or on departure.

payments.text: The UK Foreign Office says Libya is a cash-based society and you cannot use bank cards at banks, ATMs or hotels; that there is a severe shortage of cash and the Libyan Central Bank has imposed restrictions on cash withdrawals; that exchange is tightly controlled by the Central Bank, no bank will change money, exchange offices approved by the Central Bank operate at black market rates, and informal methods of exchange carry the risk of arrest; and that it is illegal to take dinar out of Libya.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Libya except the cities of Tripoli, Misrata, and Benghazi, Al-Bayda, Derna and the surrounding Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those cities. It says the security situation remains dangerous and unpredictable, citing localised violence between competing armed groups, kidnap, detention, and a high risk of striking unexploded bombs or mines off-road, and says in-person support is not available in Libya.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Libya except the cities of Tripoli, Misrata, and Benghazi, Al-Bayda, Derna and the surrounding Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those cities. It says it is a realistic possibility that terrorist groups will target foreign nationals for kidnap, and that in-person UK government support is not available in Libya: the British Embassy in Tunis provides assistance.

Libya's eVisa portal says that for a tourist visa the sponsor (the tourism company) must be registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority and hold a delegate card, and that a copy of the tourism company's letter identifying the tourist group and the destination of the visit must be uploaded to the system.

The UK Foreign Office says there is a UN-facilitated ceasefire in place between eastern and western armed forces, but there is still a high risk of localised violence between competing armed groups throughout the country, and that the Interim Government of National Unity has limited control of security provision across the country.
The UK Foreign Office says bank cards cannot be used at banks, ATMs or hotels, no bank will change money, and it is illegal to take dinar out of Libya.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Libya?
faq.answer: Yes, unless you hold an Algerian, Malaysian, Mauritanian or Tunisian passport, which the country list behind Libya's eVisa portal marks as fully exempt; it marks Türkiye as partially exempt. The portal lists the tourist visa with an "Apply now" link and says the sponsor (the tourism company) must be registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority.

faq.question: Is Libya open for tourism?
faq.answer: Libya's eVisa portal lists the tourist visa with an "Apply now" link and says the sponsor (the tourism company) must be registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority. The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Libya except the cities of Tripoli, Misrata, and Benghazi, Al-Bayda, Derna and the surrounding Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those cities.

faq.question: Does Libya have an eVisa or visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Libya's eVisa portal lists the tourist visa with an "Apply now" link, sponsored by a tourism company registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority, and says online applications for its other visa types are not open yet. No official source we could read describes a visa on arrival.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Libya?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Libya except the cities of Tripoli, Misrata, and Benghazi, Al-Bayda, Derna and the surrounding Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those cities. It says the security situation remains dangerous and unpredictable, that violence can break out with little warning, and that it is a realistic possibility that terrorist groups will target foreign nationals for kidnap, and that criminal gangs also carry out kidnappings.

faq.question: Can I enter Libya with an Israeli passport or Israeli stamps?
faq.answer: No official source we could read states the rule for Israeli passports. The UK Foreign Office says that if your passport shows previous travel to Israel, it will not be accepted for travel to Libya, and the Government of Canada says you may be denied entry if your passport bears an Israeli visa or border stamp.

countryFacts.payments.text: Libya is a cash-based society. You cannot use bank cards at banks, ATMs or hotels.
It is illegal to take dinar out of Libya.
There is a severe shortage of cash in Libya, and the Libyan Central Bank has imposed restrictions on cash withdrawals throughout the country.
The exchange of foreign currency into Libyan dinar is tightly controlled by the Libyan Central Bank.

You can legally use exchange offices approved by the Central Bank, but they operate at black market rates. No bank will change money. Informal methods of currency exchange exist though their use carries the risk of arrest.

countryFacts.bestTimeToVisit.text: In the north, near the Mediterranean coast, summers are hot and dry, and winters are rainy. In the south, the climate is semi-arid, and it can get very hot in the Sahara, especially in summer. Between June and September, temperatures can exceed 40°C, and sand and dust storms are frequent.

entryRequirements.postArrivalRegistratio.text: All short-stay visitors must register with the police within a week of arrival. The company you’re visiting or the local travel agency you’re using will usually arrange this. If you do not register, you could get a fine when you leave the country.
If you travel to Libya despite our advice, you must register your passport with a police station on arrival.
If it's safe to do so, go to the police station closest to the place you're staying. Failure to do so may result in fines and problems during your stay or on departure.
